title: The Sun Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Sun upright: joy, clarity, warmth; reversed: muted joy. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it for your question.
image_alt: The Sun, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a naked child with a red feather in a flower wreath rides a white horse under a large sun with a face, an orange-red banner and sunflowers behind a wall.
capsule: The Sun, card XIX of the Major Arcana, stands for joy, success and optimism, with clarity and warmth. Reversed, the light is still there but muted by tiredness or self-doubt. It is a good card with one small request: let yourself enjoy it. Nothing in the bright scene is hidden, so the upright answer is a clear yes.

blocks.heading: What is on The Sun card?
paragraphs: A huge sun with a calm human face fills the top half of the card. Below it a child rides a white horse with both arms flung open. Waite describes "the naked child mounted on a white horse and displaying a red standard" and calls this the better symbolism for the card (p. 144). On the 1909 card the standard is a long orange-red cloth curling beside the horse, the child wears a wreath of flowers with a red feather, and XIX is printed at the top.

Behind the rider runs a gray stone wall with sunflowers rising over it. Waite reads the scene as a road: the child is the light that goes before "the endless procession of humanity, coming out from the walled garden of the sensitive life and passing on the journey home" (p. 144).

Older decks drew something else. Waite recalls two children inside a walled garden, "gambolling, or running hand in hand" (pp. 27–28), while the lone rider with a scarlet standard is named there as "a much better symbol" (p. 28). He also notes that older cards gave the sun chief rays "waved and salient alternately" (p. 27); on the 1909 card, too, wavy rays take turns with straight ones.

The sun itself is the largest thing in the picture. Waite calls it "the glorious sun of earth" and, in a deeper sense, the light "of consciousness in the spirit", direct light as opposed to reflected light (p. 144).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Sun?
paragraphs: Waite's list for this card is short and plainly cheerful: well-being in everyday life, a happy marriage, contentment. The reversed side does not flip the meaning; it keeps the same good news at a lower volume.
His own attention went to the child. He wrote that in his simplicity the child "bears the seal of Nature and of Art", and that in his innocence "he signifies the restored world" (p. 147).

blocks.heading: What does The Sun mean upright?
paragraphs: Joy without complications is the heart of The Sun: things look clear, warm and easy to understand. It often shows up when something is going well, or when you are finally able to see the good that was already there. The child on the horse has nothing to hide and nothing to prove, and the card offers you the same ease. Success is part of the card too: effort that pays off, recognition, a stretch when things go your way and optimism comes easily.

Clarity is its second gift. Under this light the shape of a situation is plain, so it gets easier to say what you want and to act with confidence. Waite's contentment belongs here too: not a grand win, just the sense that today is enough.
The question the card leaves you with is a light one: what is going well right now, and how could you enjoy it without waiting for a catch?

blocks.heading: What does The Sun mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Sun keeps its warmth but loses some shine. What remains is a muted joy, real but dimmed, perhaps by tiredness, perhaps by self-doubt that tells you not to celebrate too soon. It can also mean feeling down for a while, success arriving more slowly than hoped, or optimism that runs ahead of the facts. It is closer to passing clouds on a summer afternoon than to a change in the weather.
Here the modern reading and Waite meet: his reversed line is "the same in a lesser sense" (p. 286). The tiredness and self-doubt are a modern reading, not Waite's.
Pick one bright moment in your day and give it your full attention, without explaining it away.

blocks.heading: What does The Sun mean in love?
paragraphs: Laughing together, saying your plans out loud, letting affection show in small daily ways: in a relationship, The Sun brings this kind of warmth, play and openness. Few cards are happier for love: it stands for a bond that feels secure, glad and in harmony, where small shared pleasures count as much as big gestures.

On your own, the card can point to a new romance that feels light and fun, to the ease of being yourself around new people, enjoying a conversation without rehearsing every line, and letting lightness lead.
The reversed side here is gladness kept in reserve, as if you need certainty before you relax. Where could you let a little more light in?

blocks.heading: What does The Sun mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Effort that shows, tasks that feel clear and success that others notice make a sunny stretch at work. The card favors working in the open: sharing results, asking plainly for what you need, taking credit without shrinking it.

Abundance and a comfortable stretch are what The Sun brings to money: bills covered, a sense of financial security, the relief of seeing the numbers add up. It describes money going well, not a windfall.
In reverse, fatigue can make good work seem smaller than it is; watch for that.

blocks.heading: What is The Sun's advice?
paragraphs: Spend some time in daylight doing something that makes you laugh or feel playful. Let gladness be simple, with no reason or permission required. Even a short walk outside with no errand attached counts.

blocks.heading: Is The Sun a yes or no card?
The Sun as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Drawn for a person, The Sun shows someone open and warm, easy company, at home in plain view. Your own version is the side of you that shines once you stop hiding. For feelings, The Sun carries one of the warmest meanings in the deck: sincere affection, happiness in each other's company, love that is shown openly rather than kept secret. Reversed, the warmth is still real but dimmed: affection held back, a cheerfulness that is genuine but low on fuel, or feelings not yet put into words.

pairs.text: After a foggy stretch, things come into view. Check what is real, then enjoy seeing it plainly.
Joy that wants company. Celebrate with your people, even over something small.
Success other people can see. Accept the credit instead of brushing it off.
Light falls on a trap that was mostly in your head. Notice which limit you could step out of first.

blocks.heading: The Sun or The Star?
paragraphs: Both cards are bright and hopeful. The Star, in Waite's description, shows "a great, radiant, star of eight rays, surrounded by seven lesser stars" above a woman who pours water from two ewers onto sea and land (p. 136); today it is read as quiet hope and calm after a hard time. The Sun is full daylight: joy that is already here rather than hoped for. Breathing easier again leans toward The Star; simply enjoying what is in front of you is The Sun.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Sun
paragraphs: What is going well for me that I have not stopped to enjoy?
Where am I hiding a part of myself that could be seen?
What small thing could I celebrate today?

faq.q: Is The Sun a good or bad card?
faq.a: Good, and one of the most openly positive cards in the deck. It backs joy, clear sight and honesty about what you want. If it asks anything, it is that you don't hold off on a good moment while you wait for something to spoil it.

Not as a prediction. Waite's 1911 list does include "fortunate marriage" (p. 286), but Arcana Diary reads no events into the card. Here The Sun speaks about warmth and openness in your own way of loving, whatever shape your relationships take.

faq.q: Who is the child on The Sun card?
faq.a: Waite gives him no name. He writes that the light of the card is "typified by the heart of a child" and that this child stands for simplicity, and for innocence in the sense of wisdom (pp. 144, 147). Read today, he is the part of anyone that can still enjoy something without needing a reason.

faq.q: Does The Sun mean he loves me?
faq.a: As a meaning, it is about as glad an answer as a card can give. The Sun traditionally stands for open, happy affection, the kind that is easy to see and does not play games. Reversed, that fondness is quieter or held in. Either way the card names a meaning, not a fact about one particular person.

waite.quote: Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment. Reversed: The same in a lesser sense.
